title: SCHOOLED: New Rules for State Mandates
author: Michael J. Petrilli
summary: Michael Petrilli follows up on his earlier question about when states should override local control, collecting reader responses to his three proposed commandments for state mandates. The commandments say mandates fit when evidence is overwhelming, when they are easy to implement and enforce, and when there is an intractable barrier to local action. Respondents suggest minimum starting teacher salaries, differential pay for high-need schools, K-2 screening, and instructional-day minimums, while others warn about input-based accountability, the limits of mandating quality, and unfunded play-based learning laws. He then turns to what a possible blue wave could mean for state education reform and school choice, drawing on views from several state advocates and on ten commitments from a coalition of left-of-center groups. He ends with a newsletter of linked reading from the week.
points: Petrilli's three-part test for state intervention is evidence, enforceability, and an intractable local barrier, and respondents propose adding a fourth requiring that less restrictive options be unlikely to work.
Several readers argue that states should protect conditions such as time for recess but avoid prescribing practice, and should fund coaching if they mandate play-based learning.
Simeon Stolzberg's point is that the push for mandates reflects an absence of real accountability for outcomes, which is why inputs have become the fight.
On a possible blue wave, the advocates expect choice programs to be capped and regulated more than abolished, with scale and age of programs determining how durable they are.
Petrilli praises the left-of-center ten commitments but notes that they lack state accountability systems and math goals.
quotes: What’s the limiting principle? Not just for recess but for all these other policy debates, can we come up with some kind of reasonable rules for when states should intervene versus when they should leave matters to local school boards or even school principals?

Yeah, in some states at least, I think there’s long been a case for a minimum starting teacher salary mandate—given how districts continue to fail to prioritize that, versus endless increases in total staffing.
The focus on and fight over these inputs has almost completely blinded parents, educators, and politicians alike to the unconscionable outcomes of so many of our schools.
Your question about a limiting principle got me thinking about something Rick Hess often says: Policymakers can make people do things, but they can’t make them do them well.
I believe states can reasonably protect a condition, like a floor on time, but get into trouble when they try to legislate practice.
A mandate without support and a way to monitor it is a recipe for poor and uneven implementation!
The easier path for choice-skeptical Dems is to cap, regulate, and quietly stifle choice programs.
If past is prologue, a blue wave will likely accelerate the red state-blue state divergences in education.
